passage:
'Did you hear about Rupa and that manager?' Jasleen asked her sister, drying the steel plates.
'Mm. Mausi told me.' Alka shook her head. 'But why did she keep going to those late meetings? Why did she let it go on for months?' She stopped, a plate in her hand. 'Wait. Listen to me.'
'What?'
'I'm asking what Rupa did wrong. She didn't make him send those messages at midnight. She didn't make him threaten her appraisal.'
Jasleen leaned on the counter. 'So what's the real question?'
'Who had the power there? He did. He chose to send them. He chose to hold her job over her head.'
Alka put the plate down. 'I'm calling Rupa tonight. Not to ask why. Just to ask how she's doing and what she needs.'
'I'll sit with you while you call,' Jasleen said.

qa.q: What did Alka say the manager chose to do?
qa.a: He chose to send the messages at midnight and chose to hold Rupa's job over her head.

qa.q: Why did Alka stop with a plate in her hand?
qa.a: She noticed that her questions were all about what Rupa did wrong, and it bothered her that she was blaming the person who was hurt.

qa.q: What did Alka decide once she changed her question?
qa.a: She decided to call Rupa that night just to ask how she was doing and what she needed, instead of asking why she let it go on.

qa.q: How might Rupa feel if the call began with 'why did you keep going to those meetings'?
qa.a: Rupa would probably feel judged and ashamed, and might stop telling her family anything about the manager.

grounding: A woman catches herself asking why Rupa let harassment continue and turns the question to who held power and chose to act.

passage: Last month my flatmate Jaya came home shaking; two men on a bike had snatched her phone outside the metro station. My first words, and I'm not proud of them, were, "Why were you holding it out on that road? You know that stretch." She went quiet and took her tea to her room. I'm Uma, and I've always thought of myself as the practical one. That night I lay awake replaying it. Jaya didn't grab her own phone and ride away with it. Two men planned it, waited for someone distracted, and chose to do it. My question had quietly put her on trial. The next morning I knocked, sat on her floor, and said, "I'm sorry. They did this, not you." Then I helped her fill in the police complaint.

qa.q: What happened to Jaya outside the metro station?
qa.a: Two men on a bike snatched her phone outside the metro station.

qa.q: Why did Uma lie awake that night replaying the conversation?
qa.a: Uma felt uneasy that the first question had put Jaya on trial instead of the two men, which clashed with how Uma wanted to treat a friend.

qa.q: What did Uma choose to do the next morning, and why might it help Jaya?
qa.a: Uma apologised, told Jaya "They did this, not you," and helped with the police complaint, taking the blame off Jaya and giving practical help.

qa.q: What might Jaya have felt when she took her tea to her room?
qa.a: Jaya probably felt hurt and blamed, as if coming home shaken wasn't enough and she also had to defend herself 🥺.

grounding: The narrator catches a 'why did you let it happen' reaction to a robbery and shifts responsibility to the men who chose to act.

passage: Supervisor's note, Thursday. At today's shift review, Samir, our newest team lead, went through Tuesday's incident, when a delivery contractor shouted at Francis and shoved a crate at him. Samir began, "Why did Francis let it get that far? He could have walked off." Then he paused, looked at his notes, and said, "Actually, that's the wrong question. The contractor chose to shout. The contractor chose to shove the crate. What do we do about that?" The room shifted. Francis, who had kept his eyes on the table, looked up. The team agreed the contractor's firm will be informed, and loading will now have two staff present. Afterwards I thanked Samir for correcting himself in front of everyone. I also checked in with Francis privately; he said he felt heard. R. Kulkarni, shift supervisor

qa.q: What did the contractor do to Francis on Tuesday?
qa.a: A delivery contractor shouted at Francis and shoved a crate at him.

qa.q: What might Samir have realised when he paused over his notes?
qa.a: He seems to have realised that asking why Francis let it happen put the blame on the person harmed, when the contractor made the choices.

qa.q: Which decision at the review turned Samir's new question into action?
qa.a: The team agreed to inform the contractor's firm and keep two staff at loading, dealing with the person who acted rather than with Francis.

qa.q: How does Francis seem to experience the change in Samir's question?
qa.a: Francis, who had kept his eyes on the table, looked up, and later told R. Kulkarni that he felt heard.

grounding: A supervisor records a team lead replacing 'why did he let it happen' with who acted and what they chose.

passage:
Tuesday, late
Tushar came back from the client meeting grey in the face. The client, Mr Bedi, had thrown the printed report across the table and called Tushar 'useless' in front of three people.
First thing I thought, honestly: why did Tushar let him talk like that? Why not walk out? Why go alone?
I actually typed half of that into the chat before I stopped.
Tried the question the other way round. Who did something? Mr Bedi. What did he choose? To shout, to throw paper, to insult a junior in public. Tushar chose to stay calm and finish the meeting. That's the only choice on Tushar's side, and it wasn't a bad one.
Deleted my message. Sent: 'That was not okay of him. Want to tell our manager together tomorrow?'
Tushar replied: 'thanks Omkar, needed that 🙏'

qa.q: What did Mr Bedi throw across the table?
qa.a: The printed report.

qa.q: Why did 'why did Tushar let him' come to Omkar's mind first?
qa.a: It felt natural to look for what Tushar could have done differently; asking about the target's choices makes such things seem controllable and less frightening.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Omkar's evening, and what choice followed?
qa.a: Stopping halfway through typing and asking who acted and what they chose; Omkar deleted the blaming message and offered to go to the manager with Tushar.

qa.q: What would Tushar have felt if Omkar's first message had been sent?
qa.a: Tushar, already shaken, would likely have felt blamed a second time, as if the insult were Tushar's fault, and might have stayed quiet about it. 😔

grounding: An adult catches a 'why did they let it happen' thought about an insulted colleague and asks instead who acted and what they chose.

passage:
Hansa: they broke in while I was at the wedding. lock smashed, laptop gone, my nani's bangles gone
Santosh: what?? are you okay?
Hansa: I'm okay. just shaky
Santosh: why did you leave the flat empty for four days though? and no camera?
Santosh: wait. ignore that
Santosh: that's me doing the thing again. asking what you did instead of what they did
Santosh: someone chose to smash your lock and take your nani's bangles. that's on them, fully
Hansa: I've been asking myself the same 'why did I' all afternoon
Santosh: then let's both stop 🤍 have you told the police? want me to come over with a new lock and dinner?
Hansa: police came, it's filed. yes please. dal chawal?
Santosh: on my way

qa.q: What was taken from Hansa's flat?
qa.a: The laptop and Hansa's nani's bangles.

qa.q: What does Santosh's 'wait. ignore that' show about what Santosh was thinking?
qa.a: It shows Santosh felt a quick pang of regret, noticing the blaming question as a habit, 'doing the thing again', and wanted to put the responsibility back on the people who broke in.

qa.q: Which choice turned the chat around, and why did it help Hansa?
qa.a: Santosh chose to name who acted: someone chose to smash the lock and take the bangles; that let Hansa stop asking 'why did I' and accept practical help.

qa.q: If you were Hansa, how would the first 'why did you leave the flat empty' feel after a burglary?
qa.a: It would feel like blame on top of the loss, adding to the 'why did I' that had already been going round in Hansa's head all afternoon.

grounding: An adult who starts to ask why a burgled friend left the flat empty catches it and names the burglars as the ones who chose the harm.
